Claude Lanzmann [diretor de Shoah (1985)] sobre o filme de Spielberg. Muito se fala sobre Tropa de Elite (2007) ser fascista, e sim, formalmente, ele é. Só que existe uma diferença enorme entre o filme de Padilha e o de Spielberg: o primeiro é uma escabrosidade técnica; mal filmado, montado, fotografado, articulado politicamente e narrativamente; tudo naquele filme, sob o viés técnico para além de sua ideologia formal, é uma nojeira. O segundo, no entanto, é o contrário: a direção, atuações, produção, figurinos, fotografia, trilha sonora, tudo isso é da mais alta qualidade. E, claro, o detalhe mais importante que torna essa comparação uma questão hierárquica: estamos falando do diretor arauto do blockbuster; o diretor possivelmente mais prestigiado do cinema contemporâneo. Por isso, retorno ao meu texto sobre A Paixão de Cristo (2004), de Mel Gibson, tão fascista quanto. O cinema, bom ou não, ainda mais sob a influência do audiovisual como mediador de verdades e narrativas — a televisão, coisa que Spielberg, Lucas, Coppola e Scorsese ajudaram a alimentar —, molda a percepção através da forma, que aliena, que guia o sentimento do espectador. Spielberg faz exatamente isso. Com sua habilidade inegável para manipular as emoções mais fortes do espectador, A Lista de Schindler torna-se um grande morde-e-assopra. As vítimas do Holocausto são meros instrumentos da sua câmera, fotografia, decupagem e trilha opulentas; tudo isso é apenas uma muleta para que o homem nazista, diretamente causador e conivente de toda essa estrutura, se compadeça e se solidarize com o horror de que estava participando. Ou seja, o olhar humanista não é dado aos desumanizados; ele é dado a quem desumaniza, arrependido ou não. É a banalidade do mal; é o individualismo levado ao limite. Nem é preciso dizer que o filme é maniqueísta. Amon Göth é um personagem muito bem estabelecido; sua maldade, sua personalidade, visão de mundo, ameaça, representação, arquétipo. Mas como um diretor tem a coragem de unificar um sistema inteiro em uma rivalidade bilateral? Como um diretor prefere debater a moralidade de dois nazistas a dar voz àqueles a quem ela foi negada? Isso me lembra, contudo, que o cinema é feito de duas coisas: primeiramente, é objetivamente impossível que exista um filme mal filmado e montado [que funcione], porque isso significa falhar nos dois pilares essenciais que o sustentam. Segundamente, um filme precisa propor uma dialética, não falando sobre política, não defendendo lados; é preciso fazer filmes politicamente. Portanto, a forma, a parte mais essencial do discurso de cinema, deve corroborar com suas intenções políticas. Se estas são reacionárias, independente do posicionamento do autor, está é reacionária. É por isso que Tropa de Elite é um filme tão desprezível, pois falha em tudo o que há de essencial como arte e falha como sétima arte. No entanto, não consigo achá-lo pior do que Schindler , porque Schindler , embora seja feito por um diretor incomparavelmente mais habilidoso do que Padilha na hora de filmar, é um filme que só poderia ser feito por americanos, para americanos e com americanos. O filme nunca se preocupa em discutir o fascismo enquanto fenômeno político, antropológico, histórico e inevitável, mas sim em reafirmar através da forma (e é aí que mora o perigo dele) tudo o que já sabemos; e ainda tem a coragem de entregar toda a solidariedade para o salvador branco no final; porque oh!, ele deu continuidade à família tradicional! Ele semeou a continuidade da vida e graças a Deus e a pátria que o antinazifascista nos tirou da desgraça! No fim, é só o fascismo fazendo o que sempre faz: vem com discursos de socialismo, igualdade e solidariedade para com os verdadeiros significados, mas faz isso através do apagamento e da instrumentalização dessas ideias, oferecendo compaixão para com o político com poder nas mãos e uma mensagem sobre a família tradicional logo após apenas reconhecer a barbárie. Veja esse filme se você não viu. Não porque ele é bom, mas sim porque é preciso entender os EUA, é preciso entender o capitalismo, é preciso entender a política; é questionando abominações como esse filme que você realmente começa a trabalhar a sua empatia, seu pensamento crítico, sua visão de mundo e sua forma de viver. E, depois deste, veja Noite e Neblina (1956), de Alain Resnais; veja, através desse filme, a oposição a tudo o que Schindler é — portanto, um filme que sabe do poder do cinema, mas o usa como arte humanista, e não como eugenista. O filme de Resnais não quer ser hegemônico; ele não quer sequestrar as pluralidades culturais e os olhares. Nota: Por fim, só não dou zero estrelas porque nem mesmo esse fascismo merece estar sob o mesmo pódio de Bohemian Rhapsody (2018). No entanto, esta nota é profundamente egoísta, evidentemente, visto que a minha ojeriza para com esse "filme" é um tanto identitária.

09 Feb 19 Mit L. vor ein paar Tagen über Schindlers Liste gesprochen. Sie, unterm Strich, für den Film. Ich, mit Wut, spreche gegen ihn, bis mir die Tränen kommen. Filmische Ästhetisierung, hollywoodsche Dramaturgie auf der Grundlage der Shoa, das könne ich nicht akzeptieren. Sie führt an, durch die Schilderung von Einzelschicksalen werde einem das Grauen wieder neu begreiflich. Ich verstehe das, nur – und vielleicht bin ich dadurch ungerecht – ich brauche das nicht. In jeder Einzelheit, die ich von der Shoa erfahre, und seien es nur statistische Daten, kapituliere ich vor diesem Grauen. Und filmisch zu insinuieren, dies Grauen sei einem tatsächlich begreiflich, halte ich, wenn nicht für unredlich, so doch für einen Irrtum. Der Film kokettiert mit dem Triumph der Menschlichkeit, wo die Shoa genau das Gegenteil bezeugt hat, nämlich den Untergang, die völlige Vernichtung von Menschlichkeit. Man kann von der Shoa erzählen, Kertész, Levi oder Begley haben es bewiesen. Und obwohl gerade sie alles Recht dazu gehabt hätten, haben sie es ohne Rührseligkeit getan; ihnen hat sich der Kitsch verboten, weil er sich in den Lagern verboten hat. Auch in ihren Werken waltet die Menschlichkeit, und vielleicht nicht nur ex negativo, aber sie ist bei ihnen keine dramaturgische Erbmasse. Wie Spielberg über die Frage, ob nun Wasser oder Gas aus den Duschen komme, einen cineastischen Tonus generiert – das ist degoutant, und es ist gefährlich, weil er die Shoa popkulturell trivialisiert. Das gesteht L. zu: dass der Film emotionalisiere. Darin sei aber auch eine Möglichkeit, sich aus der konditionierten Abschottung gegen das Thema zu lösen. Dagegen fällt mir nichts ein. Aber ich beharre darauf: nicht auf diese Weise. Ich könne es nicht hinnehmen, dass der Film die historische Wirklichkeit frisiere zum Zwecke dramaturgischer Effekte, die auch noch das Falsche ableiten. Der Film will Hoffnung aus der Shoa schöpfen – diese leichtsinnige Perversion verkrafte ich nicht. Hier kann man nicht sagen: Es sei eben Hollywood, da müsse man Konzessionen machen. Nein. Hier gerade nicht.

A popularização do cinema no início do século XX traz consigo possivelmente um dos elementos mais importantes da sociedade moderna: uma nova autoridade sobre a verdade. Veja, nos períodos anteriores a invenção da câmera, a constatação de um evento da realidade era confirmada a partir da pintura, escultura e da escrita em pedra e papel, porém, esses meios estão sujeitos a todo tipo de falsificação e manipulação daqueles que o portam ou fabricam; uma pintura não é um retrato totalmente confiável de um acontecimento, do mesmo jeito que uma escultura e um documento escrito não podem ser confirmados de sua veracidade justamente por sempre trazer o viés daquele que o cria. Somente com a chegada do cinema e sobretudo da câmera, a realidade pôde ser por sua completude registrada, afinal, a câmera apenas registra aquilo que está a sua frente, trazendo assim um enorme poder para a imagem como a autoridade da verdade. Entretanto, o cinema traz uma natureza sedutora para a imagem; iluminação, atuação, movimentação da câmera entre outros elementos criam uma experiência que é fácil de crer, se perder e de se emocionar. Evidentemente, esses elementos trazem justamente à tona, o que a imagem anteriormente havia superado, a manipulação da realidade. Quando Truffaut diz que "Não existe filme anti-guerra" , se referia justamente a essa ideia, a câmera do cinema é sedutora por natureza, não há como retratar um evento político tão devastador como uma guerra sem, mesmo que sem intenção, enaltece-la. A natureza da imagem é atraente, a história é reescrita por um número de roteiristas, o conflito passa a se tornar heroico e a guerra acaba virando apenas um palco para expor a habilidade técnica daquele que a transforma em narrativa. O holocausto cria um momento divisivo na história, pela primeira vez desde a invenção da câmera, não haviam registros históricos de um acontecimento da realidade, a Alemanha proibiu que qualquer tipo de fotografia fosse tirada do evento, logo, se não há imagem, não há verdade, não há realidade. Mas bem, o holocausto aconteceu, as pessoas morreram nos campos de concentração, surge-se então, depois da segunda guerra mundial um dilema: como registrar o holocausto? Ademais, como registrar o holocausto sem torná-lo sedutor? Tendo em vista a natureza atraente da imagem. Comparado a sua geração, Spielberg é possivelmente um dos diretores mais técnicos da época, não a toa, iniciou a era de filmes blockbuster em Hollywood. Porém, diferente de Tubarão, E.T, Indiana Jones, entre outros filmes do diretor, torna-se necessário um cuidado a mais ao se tratar de um tópico tão delicado quanto o holocausto. Não há problema, em um filme qualquer, no ato de editar uma música triste no momento de tragédia, ou uma música feliz no momento de felicidade, porém ao fazer isso em um contexto de guerra real, onde famílias inteiras foram mortas, cria-se um senso de heroísmo para a imagem, seduzindo aquele que a assiste. Imputando, até, heroísmo para aquele que não o merece. Schindler era um capitalista nazista, usufruiu de trabalho escravo judeu e usou da guerra para enriquecer, o mesmo é, entretanto, tratado como herói, por ter salvo uma pequena parcela daquele quem ele mesmo concordou em exterminar. O contraponto, contudo, vem de forma pronta logo na publicidade do filme: baseado em uma história real. Se o holocausto não foi gravado pelo instrumento de reprodução da verdade do século, como pode qualquer ato de Schindler registrado no filme ser imputado como verdadeiro? Não estou argumentando que o filme fabricou um evento histórico e que Schindler não salvou aqueles judeus, porém, ao não existir a prova da imagem, se cria uma personalidade que pode ser moldada e fabricada por aquele que a captura. Durante todo o filme, Spielberg coloca Schindler contra os soldados alemães, criando uma dicotomia, um inimigo comum, para que desenvolva no espectador um sentimento de bravura, ao fazer entender que aquele parece ser o único homem são entre os nazistas. Evidentemente é muito fácil criar um sentimento de inimigo comum quando o inimigo são soldados da SS, mas o jeito em que Spielberg filma os judeus cria um sentimento de piedade no espectador, não que as pessoas que foram vítimas do holocausto não o mereçam, mas é feito propositalmente para enaltecer alguém igualmente hediondo na história. Por conta da proeza técnica de quem o filma, não leva muito tempo até que o sofrimento do povo judeu passe a se tornar entretenimento, não necessariamente prazeroso pelo ato do extermínio, mas sim pela natureza atraente da imagem, impulsionada pelo trabalho exímio de Spielberg em enaltecer a imagem, e que logo transforma-se em heroísmo, algo muito semelhante ao o que acontece em O Resgate do Soldado Ryan, alguns anos depois. Se há forma de criar um filme verdadeiramente anti-guerra eu não tenho certeza, entretanto, não acredito que é certo, dentro de um contexto bélico, imputar heroísmo a um agente igualmente danoso à aqueles o opõe, ademais quando o heroísmo é criado a partir da reprodução da dor de milhões de mortos.

There's something troubling about a Holocaust film in which the most fully realized, psychologically complex character is a Nazi commandant. Ralph Fiennes is extraordinary as Amon Göth, a man capable of monstrous cruelty, pathetic self-pity, and moments of almost banal insecurity. His performance is terrifying precisely because he never plays a monster. He plays a human being whose capacity for evil is inseparable from his ordinary weaknesses. Unfortunately, neither Schindler nor the Jewish characters receive comparable attention. Liam Neeson's Schindler is an appealing but rather schematic figure, his transformation from opportunistic businessman to humanitarian following a predictable trajectory. The Jewish victims, meanwhile, are too often reduced to a collective embodiment of suffering, their individuality sacrificed to the film's enormous emotional ambitions. Ben Kingsley's Itzhak Stern offers some resistance to this tendency, but even he functions primarily as Schindler's moral compass. Spielberg's direction is technically masterful, yet his instinct to dramatize, sentimentalize, and provide emotional resolution seems fundamentally at odds with the enormity of his subject. The film repeatedly organizes unimaginable suffering into familiar dramatic patterns, complete with suspense, redemption, and carefully orchestrated catharsis. Nowhere is this contradiction more apparent than in the gas chamber sequence. The women are herded into a shower room, convinced they're about to be murdered. Spielberg's manipulation of space, sound, and anticipation is masterful. It's also deeply uncomfortable. He exploits our knowledge of the gas chambers to construct an almost unbearable suspense sequence, only to reward the audience with the relief of water emerging from the showerheads. It's an extraordinarily effective piece of filmmaking that leaves a distinctly bad taste. The historical reality was not a suspense thriller with a last-minute reprieve, but the systematic, mechanized murder of millions. Transforming that knowledge into a cinematic fake-out feels perilously close to using the Holocaust for audience titillation. The sequence encapsulates everything that troubles me about the film: Spielberg's technical brilliance employed in the service of an emotional manipulation that seems inappropriate to the subject. Ironically, the finest sequence comes at the very end, when the film abandons its dramatic reconstruction and allows the surviving Schindlerjuden to appear as themselves, placing stones on Schindler's grave. For a few minutes, the distance between representation and historical reality collapses. It's more affecting than much of what precedes it. *Schindler's List* is undeniably accomplished, but I find its insistence on making the Holocaust emotionally accessible through conventional storytelling increasingly difficult to accept. Claude Lanzmann's *Shoah*, which refuses reenactment, dramatic consolation, and the reassuring structure of a rescue narrative, offers a far more demanding and ultimately more profound confrontation with the same history. Spielberg wants us to feel the Holocaust. Lanzmann insists that we confront it. I'd rather watch *Shoah*.

Honestly, I had this sitting at 2 stars for a while. I kept and kept thinking throughout the final minutes of the film, assessing my overall thoughts about it. I think it's easy to say that this movie is still important today, underlined by the fact a friend gave me the homework to watch this movie by the end of today, so I'm not repeating what everyone else already said about it. I think it's easiest for me if I separate the historical importance represented by this film from the film itself. As a film, this for sure is not for me, at least on a structural level, not on a thematic level, because for the latter it absolutely was for me. Not because I found it uncomfortable to watch like I was told by my friend it would be - It was in parts really interesting and as I said above, very important. But because, structurally, I really felt disappointed by this film. It definitely needs a rewatch because that's when I usually form a more confident opinion about a film especially if it's a film unlike anything else I had seen before - usually I have to get used to the structure, narrative choices, characters, and so on first, and my whole mental bandwidth is used up the first time without much space left to really dig deeper into the film. Which is why I'll definitely rewatch this film, at the latest for my Steven Spielberg rating. I also thought the movie didn't quite manage to make me feel the sheer horror and gravity of the holocaust, which I kind of expected from some scenes, yet they never really delivered. I am aware that Steven Spielberg himself said that he didn't want to make a movie that would today probably be called torture porn, but ngl, I have to disagree with him - some things need to be shown. Not excessively, but just to show to the viewer that the camera is not afraid to turn away. Which I felt like the movie did at some points. Steven Spielberg also later acknowledged the criticism that the famous acid shower scene was more dramatized movie drama than anything, and I gotta say, I disagree with that too. That scene showed the sheer horror of this part of the holocaust, and my main problem with it is that it cheaps itself out by it being a regular water shower. It's a slow-burn, and surprisingly I didn't ever really feel bored by it, so that's something at least. There was lots of stuff here where I just kind of wished to see more, and ngl, I also kind of feel ashamed of it at the same time. Not just for wanting to see more, but also for not liking this movie as much as a movie. It definitely needs a rewatch for me to truly understand all the narrative decisions made by the characters and their motivations, because as I said, most of my mental bandwidth was spent on subconsciously grasping the movie's structure, characters, and core narrative.

I will defend Spielberg harder than most, but watching this for the first time since having a fully-formed brain made me realize I don’t think this is a great movie. By trying to be both a character study and a comprehensive overview of the Holocaust, it can’t fully succeed at either. As a character study, Schindler’s arc is undercut by virtually exiting the film’s view for an hour or more in the middle. As an “unflinching” depiction of the Holocaust, it’s weighed down by being situated within a Hollywood-ized drama. It’s not that it’s necessarily sanitized, but the swelling violin score and pretty lighting make this feel overwhelmingly like a big-budget studio achievement as much or more so than a horrific document of the past. I can think of numerous films I’ve seen whose filmmaking creates a more palpable feeling of despair or revulsion, many of which are works of pure fiction. Ultimately, this film doesn’t offer a unique, challenging, or essential perspective on the Holocaust, it simply has the benefit of being the most famous, high-profile one. And yet, I can’t shake the feeling that there is value to it regardless. The Zone of Interest and Shoah aren’t exactly the type of thing the average person goes out to see on a weekend. This is an accessible, respectfully well-made general overview of the Holocaust that, at the very least, will serve a purpose forever in high school history classes. It’s not for me, but I do believe there’s a place for it.

O filme se aproxima do holocausto e o torna visualmente agradável, criando imagens esteticamente agradáveis, digo no sentido de apuração técnica, de em algumas cenas, enquadrar momentos trágicos de uma maneira tecnicamente apurada. Por exemplo, na cena em que vários corpos de judeus são incinerados, há todo um trabalho estético e técnico que torna aquilo visualmente belo, um mero estímulo emocional. A espetacularização desses eventos por si só não me parece um problema, mas sim a forma que se espetaculariza, em A Lista de Schindler, a espetacularização não funciona como uma alavanca para uma discussão temática ampla, e sim como mera ferramenta dramática, mero estímulo sensorial de tensão e choque. No filme, há uma certa individualização da criação do holocausto, que apesar de fazer com que os espectadores sintam o peso do ocorrido, acaba direcionando-os a entende-lo como um evento isolado na história, algo repulsivo porém distante, como se o holocausto fosse causa de mentes más isoladas no tempo, e não de todo um processo histórico de disseminação ideológica por parte de uma elite em crise, uma elite que quando ameaçada, foi capaz de realizar atrocidades em prol de seus privilégios. The main issue with this film is that its historical significance and humanistic subject matter can influence any cinematic assessment of it. However, if we examine it independently of its historical importance, we're left with a film that is remarkably strong in many of its formal and narrative choices, yet, as is often the case with Spielberg, doesn't quite trust itself or its audience enough when it comes to handling emotions. At the beginning of the film, Schindler is an opportunistic and ambitious businessman who exploits the political and economic circumstances for personal gain. Everything he does is driven by self interest. His transformation begins with his gradual exposure to systematic violence, but I think the screenplay focuses more on the external signs of this change than on its psychological dimensions. We see him making different decisions, but we're not given enough insight into the evolution of his perspective. As a result, the audience has to bridge some of that gap on its own, essentially having to convince itself of his transformation. The contradiction between Schindler's initial motivations and his final decisions is one of the most compelling and promising aspects of his character. However, in the second half, the film moves away from the complexity of this contradiction and gradually shifts towards constructing a moral hero. Goeth and Schindler could have represented two entirely different responses to the question of power. Both occupy positions of authority, and both benefit from the privileges offered by the system. Yet one chooses to preserve human lives, while the other uses his power to strip people of their most fundamental human rights. The problem is that Goeth occasionally stops being an independent, complex character and becomes little more than Schindler's moral opposite, despite several moments in the film where we see glimpses of a much more compelling and potentially complex character. Goeth could have had an extraordinary moral arc, one that ultimately culminated in a moral loop. Instead, he becomes a casualty of Schindler's character arc. One of Spielberg's greatest strengths is his ability to manage complex mise-en-scène and large crowds. Many sequences involve numerous actors and simultaneous movements, yet the film rarely feels chaotic. Take the liquidation of the ghetto, for example. The movements of the residents, the officers, the vehicles, and the shifting spatial arrangements are choreographed in a way that allows the audience to follow multiple layers of action simultaneously. The camera distributes information across different elements of the frame. The camera movement, high contrast, and visible film grain bring the image closer to documentary aesthetics, reinforcing its historical atmosphere. The black-and-white cinematography also creates a sense of distance between the world of the film and the conventional visual language of contemporary cinema. I also have two major criticisms. First: The film's most significant visual choice is the use of red for the little girl's coat. It's an effective visual choice, and it even serves a narrative purpose, but I personally don't see it as essential to the narrative logic of the film. The girl doesn't occupy an independent position within the film's character structure that would justify this visual distinction. Neither she nor her character is developed enough, and her presence primarily serves to create an emotional focal point for both Schindler and the audience. The narrative purpose I mentioned is that the girl marks two turning points in Oscar Schindler's transformation. His first encounter with her marks the beginning of his change, while the second becomes the final blow that completes it. And this works very well. Although, if I hadn't pointed it out just now, you probably wouldn't have noticed how necessary that connection was. My point, however, is that the red coat functions less as a character detail and more as a direct visual instruction from the director to the audience: identify this little girl among the crowd, and don't forget that she matters. It's a form of direct emotional guidance. If we changed the color of her coat to black and white while keeping the exact same shots, with perhaps a slight emphasis on her face during the second encounter, there would be virtually no dramatic difference in the film. Second: In certain moments, one of which I've already discussed, the film doesn't give the audience enough room to develop an independent emotional response. Instead, it dictates how we should feel. This reaches its peak in the film's ending, which feels both artificially constructed and unnecessarily conclusive. After saving so many lives, Schindler is overwhelmed by the realization that he could have saved even more. There's a scene in which he talks about his personal belongings, and we witness what is essentially a theatrical performance by Liam Neeson. On its own, the scene could have been a powerful ending on a conceptual level, provided it had been toned down just a little. But Spielberg doesn't stop there. He follows it with the cast and actual survivors of the Holocaust gathering around Schindler's real grave, once again emphasizing the historical and emotional significance of what we've just witnessed. This is extremely important in terms of cinema's relationship with history and collective memory. However, within the emotional structure of the film, it creates a kind of excessive emphasis. It's almost as if Spielberg doesn't trust the impact of the previous scene, or even the film as a whole, so he decides to fire one final shot just to make sure the audience gets the message.

I’ve been off work this week on some pre-planned annual leave, which has unfortunately been almost entirely wasted on being sick. I’ve basically spent the last few days either vomiting, sleeping, cleaning or feeling sorry for myself, but I’ve finally woken up feeling human again and decided that today is going to be a fuck you day. For those unfamiliar, a fuck you day involves eating absolutely anything I want, smoking some weed from midday onwards, putting my phone on Do Not Disturb and completely emptying my head of any responsibilities whatsoever. I’ve got no plans, nobody’s waiting for me to get back to them and I don’t need to do a single fucking thing. And if somebody does suddenly want something from me? Fuck you. I’ve been out and bought doughnuts, crisps, a share-size bag of peanut M&M’s, milkshake, full-fat pop, two pizzas and a shitload of bacon. I’m ready to gorge myself. I’ve decided to watch Schindler’s List . Probably not the obvious choice for this particular occasion 😅 But the Blu-ray has been staring at me for months and I’m actually a little ashamed of myself for never having seen it. I’ve been curious about whether leaving it this long might have softened the impact for me, particularly because in the 33 years since its release we’ve had films like The Zone of Interest approaching the Holocaust in such radically different ways. I think what’s surprised me most about this is how raw Spielberg has made it feel. One of my longstanding criticisms of his work is that almost everything he does has this very polished quality to it, regardless of the material and whilst that’s obviously a huge part of what makes him such an accomplished filmmaker, I tend to prefer things that feel a little rougher around the edges, particularly when the subject matter calls for it. There are shots and entire sequences here that almost feel like they’ve been accidentally captured, as though the camera has just happened to be in the right place at the right time. That was genuinely unexpected from him and I think it makes some of the violence considerably more upsetting. The opening is beautiful, those candles slowly losing their colour, the smoke rising and the transition into the trains. It’s an incredibly simple piece of filmmaking but there’s something awful about watching this entire world seemingly disappear before we’ve even met anybody. And then the restaurant sequence with Schindler is fucking brilliant. Neeson is fantastic from the beginning, he’s got this enormous presence and there’s something so entertaining about watching him walk into a room where nobody knows who he is and gradually turn himself into the most important person there. He understands exactly how to manipulate people through charm, alcohol, money and an almost ridiculous amount of confidence. It’s like watching somebody conduct a little social experiment, and what’s particularly clever is that Spielberg allows us to enjoy it despite being perfectly aware of who Schindler is trying to impress. I love that complexity in his character, particularly during the first half when his motivations are much more difficult to pin down. He’s profiting from this horrific situation and much more interested in making money than helping anybody, but he’s also capable of these little moments that suggest there’s something else going on underneath. I love stories where people aren’t particularly easy to categorise as good or bad and watching that gradual transformation into somebody genuinely trying to save lives is the strongest part of the film for me. The writing is also brilliant at showing how the occupation gradually destroys ordinary life without having to constantly explain the historical situation to us. It’s all these seemingly small practical details, people needing certain documents, businesses changing hands, names appearing on lists, somebody desperately needing a job. Things that would usually be pretty unremarkable suddenly become matters of life and death. You can actually feel the world getting smaller for these people as the film progresses. And fucking hell, some of the violence is horrible . I think the first moment that properly got to me was the one-armed worker being shot and from there it just keeps getting worse. The engineer being executed is another one, there’s something so sudden and horribly matter-of-fact about these deaths that makes them feel incredibly authentic. That sequence where the gun keeps jamming is almost unbearable too, the anticipation of what’s about to happen somehow becomes worse than the violence itself. Ralph Fiennes is astonishing in this. What an absolutely disgusting, evil presence he brings to the film, there’s something particularly frightening about a man who has almost unlimited authority over everybody within his immediate surroundings and seems perfectly comfortable exercising it whenever the fuck he feels like it. The scenes of him casually shooting prisoners are horrifying, but it’s also the little things he does that make him so unpleasant. I love that shot of Goeth washing his face whilst the windows behind him are intermittently lighting up with machine-gun fire. Incredible. His scenes with Neeson are some of my favourites too, particularly the later sequence where Goeth is drunk after the party. I think the fact that he can be swayed so easily at times actually somehow makes him seem even more evil, not really sure why that is I’ll have to think about that one. Ben Kingsley deserves just as much praise, although his performance is considerably quieter than either of the other two leads. What a ridiculous trio of actors to have at the centre of a film like this. I think that’s the advantage of having somebody like Spielberg approaching this material as a fairly conventional dramatic narrative, if you’re going to tell this story in that way then you either need a filmmaker capable of bringing every possible resource and talent to it or you need to take an enormous creative swing and approach it from somewhere completely different, like Jonathan Glazer did with The Zone of Interest . Spielberg has clearly thrown absolutely everything he’s got at this and for the most part it’s incredibly effective. There are some extraordinary visual moments throughout too. The little girl in the red coat is obviously one of the most famous images in cinema and it’s incredibly powerful, although I do wonder whether it might have had an even greater impact in 1993 than it does today, which is a pretty depressing thought in itself. Seeing that coat again amongst the dead is a fantastic moment, particularly in how it seems to cement something changing within Schindler. The sequence at Auschwitz where the women are convinced they’re about to be gassed, only for water to come out of the showerheads, is another absolutely terrifying piece of filmmaking. You can almost feel the fear radiating off the screen. John Williams is excellent here too, obviously. His music has such an enormous emotional presence without needing to dominate every scene, and I think the film really benefits from Spielberg knowing when to let the images and performances do the work instead. I do have some issues with the length though and it’s a strange criticism to make because I don’t think there’s necessarily anything here that feels completely unnecessary. It’s more that the film manages to achieve so much by around the halfway point that I started wondering whether you needed another 90 minutes of material, was it actually adding much to the experience. I think a slightly tighter version might have been even more devastating, particularly because the film is so effective when it’s concentrating on those smaller human moments rather than constantly expanding the scale. I’m also a little conflicted about the final stretch. Schindler breaking down before he flees is clearly intended to be this enormous emotional release and it is upsetting, but I found it slightly too melodramatic for my tastes. I think something more restrained might have been even more powerful considering how much of the film has relied on these relatively quiet shifts in his character. Spielberg is obviously a master of this kind of big emotional moment, but occasionally I do wish he’d trust the audience to get there without pushing quite so hard. The final images are another matter though. Spielberg has always been particularly good at endings that allow everything you’ve just watched to finally settle emotionally and there’s something incredibly moving about bringing us out of the dramatic recreation and into the real world, seeing the actual people whose lives were affected by everything we’ve spent the last 3 hours watching. I think that’s probably the part I’ll remember most vividly. After all the extraordinary filmmaking, performances and horrifying violence, seeing those people standing there brings a completely different weight to the whole experience. It’s difficult to find much to say about that really.

A lista de Schindler é sem dúvidas um filme para sempre. O filme dirigido por Spielberg conta a história real de Oskar Schindler, um alemão filiado ao partido Nazista que salvou mais de 1.000 judeus. A primeira hora é focada em Oskar e sua visão empreendedora. De início não simpatizamos com o personagem, que não passa de um homem de negócios que se aproveita da situação para fazer dinheiro, mas ainda assim, trata os judeus como humanos. Na segunda hora, o filme mostra o horror do Holocausto, a ida dos judeus ao "gueto" e depois aos campos de concentração. O filme nos apresenta Goeth, um capitão nazista que sente prazer em matar. É sem dúvidas um dos personagens que mais causa ódio no expectador na história do cinema. Loucura pensar que um homem desses existiu. Do meio pro fim, vemos a bondade de Oskar, que decide comprar os judeus para salvá-los, gastando toda sua fortura. Entre tantas cenas memoráveis, a de Oskar se martirizando porque poderia ter salvado mais vidas e a cena final das pessoas reais mexeu muito comigo. A lista de Schindler é a obra-prima de Spielberg e a melhor atuação da carreira de Liam Neeson ( que mereceu muito o Oscar). É um daqueles filmes que nos marcam e nos fazem refletir sobre os horrores do holocausto. É tão chocante que espero não vê-lo novamente. NOTA: 8.5 LUÍS EDUARDO DE PAIVA GOMES

Ben Kingsley’s Itzhak Stern was the anchor for me. There’s something so quiet and deeply human about his performance that grounds the entire film. Neeson is excellent too, while Fiennes is appropriately chilling. Six million is an impossible number to comprehend, so the film makes you look at individuals instead. Heavy, horrifying, beautiful and unforgettable. Cinema at its most devastating.

While Steven Spielberg isn’t my favorite among the legendary directors, Schindler’s List is an undeniable force. On this viewing, I found myself particularly drawn to the expert filmmaking on display. Time and again throughout its three hour runtime, Spielberg uses the medium to great narrative effect. For example, the intercutting between Jewish families being forcibly removed from their homes and sent to the ghettos and Schindler taking possession of a newly vacated apartment is brilliantly executed and effective. I do feel, however, that Spielberg occasionally overindulges in filmmaking tendencies that are deeply inappropriate given the subject matter. Most notably, the gas chamber fake-out scene near the end is egregious, emotionally manipulative, and deeply inappropriate. It’s followed roughly five minutes later by yet another fake-out involving a family separation. These are moments when Spielberg should have shown restraint. He would have done a greater service to the horrific history of the Holocaust by either committing to depicting the brutality in full or avoiding these manipulative setups entirely. At its worst, Schindler’s List is overindulgent and loses sight of itself. At its best, it is a brutally honest look at Nazi crimes and Jewish resistance.

Simplemente una joya. Aquí se puede ver claramente cómo a la SS no le importaba nada más que demostrar el odio que sentían hacia los judíos, polacos y demás grupos perseguidos. No les importaba en absoluto la vida de personas inocentes, cuyo único delito era ser judías. Los perseguían, los aislaban y los despojaban de todo, tratándolos como si no valieran absolutamente nada. En esta película se muestran un poco más de cerca los horrores que cometían contra ellos: las fosas comunes que escondían tantas atrocidades, los soldados que se hicieron ricos a costa de sus pertenencias. Les quitaron sus casas, objetos de valor e inclusive hasta los dientes de oro. He investigado mucho sobre el tema de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, sobre todo acerca de este capítulo de la historia, y me duele ver cómo se replica tanto de esto actualmente con Palestina. Recuerdo aquella fotografía de los supervivientes del Holocausto que viajaban en el Exodus 1947 rumbo a Palestina, llevando una pancarta con un mensaje que decía: (Los alemanes destruyeron nuestras familias y nuestros hogares; no destruyan también nuestras esperanzas). Es inevitable pensar en lo que representa esa imagen cuando vemos lo que sucede actualmente con el pueblo palestino. Me duele pensar que, después de haber sufrido semejantes atrocidades, sigamos siendo testigos de tanto sufrimiento y deshumanización. Me resulta inaceptable que haya personas que sigan diciendo que lo que sucede en Palestina es simplemente una guerra, cuando estamos hablando de un genocidio, de vidas inocentes, familias destruidas y de Gaza completamente devastada. Que se llegue al punto de proponer horcas para ejecutar a palestinos y que haya quienes incluso celebren estas cosas y las transmitan me parece simplemente inhumano. Es verdaderamente doloroso ver que la historia parece no enseñarnos nada. Que después de todo lo ocurrido durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial sigamos presenciando atrocidades semejantes. Al final, cobra todavía más sentido aquella frase: (Quien no conoce su historia está condenado a repetirla).

Schindler's List is a monumental achievement. The movie was filmed partly as a documentary with lots of handheld footage that gives it a sense of realism, but also as a polished, perfectly lit 40s movie where hard shadows and shafts of light across the eyes give it a classic noir look. Despite its hefty runtime it flies by, never feeling its length due to its captivating plot. The first act could almost be described as fun, with scenes of Schindler bribing and scheming his way to success playing out like one of those businessman biopics like The Founder or Air. But the film is also an unflinching, harrowing portrayal of the Holocaust that makes one squirm in their seat dreading what atrocity will be depicted next. Every actor in the movie is excellent and one struggles to comprehend how both Liam Neeson and Ralph Fiennes haven’t won any Oscars for their tremendous performances. Still, it might be Ben Kingsley that was snubbed the most as he wasn't even nominated for a role he embodied with perfection. Everyone should see this film.
